title: Can AI Help With Formative Assessment?
author: Becky Allen
summary: Prompted by Dylan Wiliam's claim that LLMs lack a "model of cognition" and are therefore weak at formative feedback, Becky Allen designed a small summer experiment to test whether a modern LLM can act as if it understands what a student is thinking. She scaffolded a "Diagnostic Tutor" GPT to parse a photographed piece of incorrect student work, build a tiny knowledge graph of the concepts involved, propose testable misconceptions with supporting evidence, and generate discriminating follow-up questions. Testing it across roughly 20 examples in subjects including biology and religious education, she found the LLM performed strongly in structured domains (maths, science, languages) where the causal space of likely errors is small, but needed tighter anchoring in interpretive domains like literature and history. She argues LLMs may hold enough "collective pedagogical content knowledge," absorbed from everything educators have written, to function diagnostically -- not because they possess genuine cognition, but because the functional test that matters is behavioural: does the system act as if it understands.
points: Allen reframes Wiliam's "model of cognition" objection as an empirically testable, behavioural question -- can the system sort a wrong answer into credible misconception hypotheses and generate probes that discriminate between them -- rather than a philosophical dead end.

Her four-step scaffold (parse and summarise, build a tiny knowledge graph, name testable misconceptions with evidence, propose discriminating probes) is a reusable structure any teacher could adapt for their own diagnostic prompting.

The domain split is the paper's most practically useful finding: the LLM performed well in structured domains like maths, science, and languages where the space of plausible errors is small, but needed tighter anchoring (exemplars, background texts) in interpretive domains like literature and history.

Allen's proposed classroom routine -- students photograph or type responses, a diagnostic tutor infers misconceptions, and the teacher gets a summary of common versus individual gaps -- explicitly keeps the teacher setting pacing and pedagogy rather than ceding the class to AI.
quotes: They don't have a model of cognition. They don't know what it is the students are thinking.
No matter how experienced the teacher, formative assessment always runs into the same problem: diagnosis at scale.

LLMs may indeed operate only as probabilistic models over text. They may not possess a model of cognition. But, as with teachers, I think the functional test is a behavioural one: does the system act as if it has a useful cognitive model?
In theory, LLMs could access everything educators have ever written about teaching: examiner reports, guides, textbooks, research papers, and online forums. This is collective PCK at scale.
Overall, the LLM performed well in diagnosing misconceptions in the pieces of work I gave it, particularly in the structured domains of maths, science, and languages.
The teacher still sets pacing and pedagogy. The model handles the piece best done as one-to-one diagnostic marking, for situations where a mini-whiteboard can’t tell the whole story.
